note: Focuses on enforcement capacity rather than drafting, on the argument that regulation without enforcement is nothing, and recommends a model for coordinating supranational and national bodies.
title: A Robust Governance for the AI Act: AI Office, AI Board, Scientific Panel, and National Authorities

reading.body:
Enforcement capacity, not regulatory text, determines whether the EU AI Act functions as intended, and coordinating supranational bodies with national authorities is essential to achieve consistent implementation across member states.

The EU created new AI rules but left open a critical question: who enforces them, and how do they work together? This paper maps the institutional landscape, identifying roles for the European Commission, the AI Office, national authorities, and a proposed Scientific Panel. The authors argue that regulatory design fails without corresponding enforcement infrastructure. Fragmented oversight across member states risks uneven compliance, where some jurisdictions enforce rigorously while others lag.

For AI scaling, this matters because regulatory uncertainty directly affects infrastructure investment. Data centers and power systems require long-term planning. Companies cannot efficiently allocate resources if enforcement expectations shift by country or if national authorities interpret rules differently. Inconsistent enforcement also creates arbitrage opportunities, where AI builders migrate workloads to permissive jurisdictions rather than solving compliance challenges at the technical level.

This paper does not evaluate whether the EU's specific enforcement model will work in practice, nor does it address implementation timelines, funding for enforcement bodies, or staffing challenges. It proposes structure but does not measure capacity. The relationship between enforcement strength and actual AI compute deployment remains empirical and will emerge only as national authorities begin enforcement actions.

explain_beginner: Europe passed a big new law for artificial intelligence, but a law only matters if someone actually checks whether companies follow it. This paper is about who does that checking. It maps out four different bodies the EU created or relies on, a new AI Office inside the European Commission, an AI Board that represents each country, a Scientific Panel of independent experts, and national watchdog authorities in each member state. The authors ask whether this setup can actually work, given how many institutions have to cooperate. They find real gaps, for example no clear referee when a national authority in one country makes a call other countries disagree with. The paper does not prove the system will fail, it proposes fixes, but it is upfront that some of its own fixes might turn out to be politically impossible to adopt in practice.
explain_business: For companies operating AI systems across the EU, this paper warns that enforcement will not be uniform in the AI Act's early years. Because the AI Board cannot currently override a national regulator, a general purpose AI model or high risk system could face a compliance action in one member state without triggering the same response elsewhere, exactly what happened when Italy suspended ChatGPT unilaterally in 2023. Businesses should expect to deal with national market surveillance authorities directly for most high risk compliance questions, while the AI Office handles general purpose model obligations centrally. Budget for regulatory unevenness during this early implementation period, since the authors argue the same resourcing gaps that hurt early GDPR enforcement, wealthier member states funding stronger regulators than smaller ones, are likely to repeat here as AI Act obligations phase in through 2025 and 2026.
explain_practitioner: Novelli and colleagues map the enforcement architecture of the EU AI Act across four layers, the AI Office, handling harmonized implementation, standardization support, regulatory sandboxes, and direct oversight of general purpose AI models, the AI Board, a member state advisory body coordinating national regulators, the Scientific Panel, independent experts supporting general purpose AI risk classification, and national market surveillance authorities, the frontline compliance checkers for high risk systems. Comparing this to GDPR's structure, they identify a specific gap, unlike the European Data Protection Board, the AI Board cannot overrule or harmonize a national authority's decision, the kind of inconsistency that let Italy unilaterally suspend ChatGPT in 2023 while other states did not act. The authors propose closer integration and dispute resolution powers, but concede their own proposal has weaknesses, including the risk that a more independent AI Office could drift from Commission priorities, and that merging the Scientific Panel with the overlapping Advisory Forum may be politically infeasible.
